title: Vow of Repentance
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan emphasizes the importance of taking responsibility for one's past actions by acknowledging and transforming their own karma, rather than seeking external forgiveness or blame. This practice, known as the vow of repentance, involves recognizing and letting go of self-loathing and delusion, allowing us to move forward with renewed awareness and compassion. By embracing this practice, we can transcend our dualistic thinking and return to a state of original nature, free from the burdens of good and bad actions.

Thank you, David, for fixing me.

Now?

So let's say it together.

*I now fully avow*

*All my ancient twisted karma* *From beginningless greed, hate, and delusion* *Born through body, speech, and mind* *I now fully avow*
*All my ancient twisted karma* *From beginningless greed, hate, and delusion* *Born through body, speech, and mind* *I now fully avow*
It's the verse of repentance, and it's sometimes called the verse of atonement.
It turns up from time to time in our Zen way.
It comes from Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
We don't talk too much about Samantabhadra, whose name means, among other things, universal virtue or universal goodness.
We talk a lot about Manjushri Bodhisattva, wisdom, and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, compassion.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva represents wisdom in action, and I emphasize action.
Samantabhadra is, at different times, a male or a female deity, and says that there can be no wisdom if it doesn't benefit beings.
Wisdom must be practiced.
She's mentioned in the Lotus Sutra, and she's also mentioned in the Avatamsaka Sutra.
Vow number four of ten vows is the vow of repentance.
The words of the vow are:
*From beginningless time I have acted unskillfully* *With craving, hatred, and ignorance* *In actions of body, speech, and mind.* *Determined now to begin anew, I repent.*
It's very easy to see how we get our vow of repentance from this, because the words are almost the same.
It is repentance, our verse and our ceremony of repentance, that I'm here to talk about.
Now the word repentance brings up baggage for a lot of people.
Maybe some of you grew up Catholic, and some of you witnessed preachers in the street shouting, "Repent, sinner!"
Or a confessional to a priest to whom you confess your sins and seek forgiveness.
So we get to sit with that a little bit.
The verse of repentance has deep meaning for me personally.
I don't know about you, but I have been visited at the oddest times by past transgressions, goofs, misdeeds.
After learning this verse I went through a long period of doing nine prostrations each morning, saying three rounds of the verse.
I remember talking it out in Dokusan with my teacher Peter Levitt at a time of feeling overwhelmed by my frailness, my frail humanity.
He pointed to the first two lines: my ancient karma from beginningless greed, hate and delusion.
It's always been there.
I didn't invent it.
We all have it.
It takes the edge off the self-loathing and self-delusion that many of us struggle with throughout our lives.
Let's relate this word karma to right now.
We don't really use karma.
We don't talk about it a lot in our Zen study, but it's about cause and effect.
I think it's the focus on now, or timelessness, that Zen chooses to focus on rather than the emphasis on past lives and past deeds.
Kri, the root of the word, means make or do, referring to a deed, but of course it is the consequences of the deed that carry over like a cloak with us in our lives.
We refer to it in our repentance as all my ancient twisted karma from beginningless greed, hate and delusion.
How do we wish to live with our karma?
We can seek to create new karma that will wipe away the old.
We can acknowledge that, past lives or not, we have inherited an infinite greed, hate and delusion.
It's been there.

We express it, born through body, speech and mind, and we can transform it by seeing it for what it is: delusion, without any nature of its own, that is the result of other delusion and thereby the acts that occur within and from that delusion.
I now fully avow.
A scholar and teacher named Sheng Yi from a modern Shaolin school says, "Karma has no nature.

As long as we don't encounter prajna or wisdom and remain unaware that karma is basically empty, if you can just concentrate your mind and transcend its falsehood and evil, the suffering of the three realms and the six states of existence will automatically disappear.
And once free from suffering, you're truly free."
In Buddhism, repentance is not about shame or guilt.
It is about acknowledging the role we play in this world and seeing it clearly.
We can express our regret, which is a way of addressing the suffering we've caused.
We can apologize if it's appropriate.
We must accept responsibility, and then we can move forward.
We want to recognize and acknowledge what we've done so we can return to the present and meet what is right here and right now.
Recognize, that's a good word.
It's an old French word.
It means to rethink, to recall to mind, to know again.
Whatever the consequences of our actions, whether wholesome or unwholesome, whether good or bad, in Buddhism we have to own them.
They're ours, and one of our jobs is to recognize that.
This is the English word avow.
"I now fully avow" means to acknowledge, to look again with eyes open, to think again, and then move forward from this place.
That is to say, to let go and return to the present.
Some of us find ourselves in that place over and over again.
There's a point where I believe we have to take responsibility for that over and over again, and just say, okay, here I am.
I'm going to walk from this place forward.
There's a story that I learned in a 12-step program, and some of you might know it.
I walked down the street.
I fell in a hole.
I walked down the same street.
I fell in the same hole.
I walked down the street again, and I tried to walk around the hole, but I still fell in.
I walked down the street, and with great effort, I tried to avoid the hole, but I fell in again.
I walked down a different street.
And that's what we have to do: walk down a different street.
If any of this sounds familiar to you, I suspect you have been practicing zazen.
When we perform the rituals or chant the repentance verse, it is not to ask forgiveness from someone else for what we've done.
It is not, "Bless me, Father, for I have sinned," which is other power.
It's important that we don't think in this way.
Ultimately, there is no gap between ourselves and the person from whom we might be asking forgiveness or whom we may have harmed, which we have committed.
Finally, when we move forward, there is also an element of repentance that encourages us to try not to create harmful consequences again.
Repentance doesn't just mean we can or should continue to cause harm or suffering.
Like I've heard so many people say, you go to confession, you confess your sins, and then you go out and do whatever you want so you can go to confession again.
That's not really how we want it to work.
Just because you can mend a broken leg doesn't mean you should break your legs.
So we take responsibility, we respect ourselves and others.
It's like that phrase we sing, giver, receiver, and gift.
We're all in it together.
We do two kinds of repentance in Zen, formal and formless.
Formal repentance is when we own up to something, usually something specific, like when we apologize for hurting someone.
Our verse of repentance, while formal, is nonspecific.
We may have a very specific repentance that we need to do.
We chant the repentance verse before ordination ceremonies, before we receive the precepts, and at the beginning of our full moon ceremony, and commitment to the precepts at that time is reaffirmed.
We chant it in our meal chant, and that's formal repentance.
The other kind of repentance we do in Zen is formless repentance.
Formless repentance is repentance in the ultimate, the absolute realm.
It's absolute, supreme, beyond any idea of good or bad, of wholesome or unwholesome, of helping or harming.
It is letting go completely.
Zazen is formless repentance exactly.
Huineng, the sixth Chinese ancestor, talked a lot about formless repentance in the Platform Sutra.
He stated that formless repentance will annihilate the sins of the past, present, and future, enabling you to attain purity of thought, word, and deed.
Formless repentance happens in each instant.
Formless repentance is manifesting your true self in this moment.
In the reality of our lives, where we live in this relative world, we have to make choices every day.
We use our discriminating mind all the time.
Even though we like to say the way is basically perfect, just avoid picking and choosing, we still have to make some decisions.
It's unavoidable.
We have to decide what is good, what is bad.
But in zazen, we just let thought pass.
No discrimination, no judgment, only pure presence.
And we are totally free from discrimination.
Repentance is letting go of our past, and zazen is letting go completely.
So our practice of zazen is also the purest, most complete form of repentance.
We need both kinds to move forward.
Formal repentance cleans the slate and softens the consequences of our self-centered actions of body, speech, and mind.
Formless repentance deals with the roots of these actions.
Formless repentance prepares us for zazen even while we're in it.

The Buddha in the Sutra of 42 Sections said, "If a person has many offenses and does not repent of them, but cuts off all thought of repentance, the offenses will engulf him, just as water returning to the sea will gradually become deeper and wider."
So it's good to repent.
Good to recognize our misdeeds.
Good to let them go and to try to do better in the future.
In Zen, whether we are working with the precepts, or sitting in zazen, or engaging in daily activity, what is emphasized is returning.
Returning to our original nature before any thoughts of separation.
Get back on the cushion.
And I love that in zazen we can't break the precepts, we can't tell a lie to somebody, we can't hurt somebody else.
We just sit in this formless place and we don't always know what's happening, but something will change.
Dogen Zenji wrote:
*We should reflect on it.
This is the exact point of a realized Buddha.
With repentance you will certainly receive invisible help from Buddha ancestors.
Repent to the Buddhas with mind and body.
The power of repentance melts the roots of unwholesomeness.
This is the single color of true practice, the true trust, the true heart of trust, the true body of trust.*
For me, sometimes hearing about these ancestors is a little confusing.
It had been very confusing.
I used to think that I couldn't figure Dogen out at all, until I figured out that you don't have to figure it out.
But on our way to Zen tonight, I was riding with Judith, and she told me about this poem that she heard from one of our Dharma brothers, Kodo, who has a small child, and had this little poem to say.
I thought if any of you want a little zazen instruction, you might take it this way.
*Zazen by heart.
The six phases of meditation in verse.*
*Find your seat and settle in.* *Make the mudra.
Tuck your chin.* *Remember why you're really here.* *To free the world from pain and fear.*
Thank you.
*Feel your breath and count to ten.* *If you get lost, you start again.* *Notice what comes up for you.* *Just let it be.
Don't think it through.* *When heart is calm and mind is bright,* *just sit within the spacious light.* *And when the meditating is done,* *send your joy to everyone.*
We can see what time we have.

In closing, I just want to say that when I was attempting to print the article that I cited at the beginning, I tried to print it twice, and ironically, my printer disgorged only the last statement of the entire article, and it is a quote from the Samantabhadra Sutra.
It says:
*The ocean of all karmic hindrances arises solely from delusive thoughts.
If you wish to make repentance, sit in upright posture and be mindful of the true reality.
All misdemeanors, like frost and dew, are melted away in the sun of wisdom.*
Thank you for listening.
We have some time, and I would like to put us into breakout rooms.
So, Joan, you're going to have to do your own breakout room.
Oh, hi, Scott.
Good.
I think we'll go into groups of three, and you can put yourselves in them, and I will send you off with three questions.
Talk about any of them.
How do you relate personally to the idea of repentance?
What is karma to you?
And what is the...
How do you relate to the idea of formal versus formless repentance?
So, find two other people to sit with.
